genesis: The book of beginnings: the creation of the world, Adam and Eve, Noah and the flood, the tower of Babel, and the families of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, ending with Israel's household settled in Egypt.
exodus: Israel enslaved in Egypt, the call of Moses at the burning bush, the plagues and the Passover, the crossing of the Red Sea, the Ten Commandments at Sinai, and the building of the tabernacle.
leviticus: The laws of worship given at Sinai: offerings and sacrifices, the priesthood of Aaron, what is clean and unclean, the Day of Atonement, the feasts of the year, and the call to be holy.
numbers: Named after its two censuses of the tribes: forty years in the wilderness between Sinai and the plains of Moab, with complaints, rebellions, the spies' report, and Balaam's blessing.
deuteronomy: Moses' farewell speeches to Israel on the border of the promised land, restating the law, with the great commandment to love God with all the heart, and ending with his death on Mount Nebo.
joshua: Israel crosses the Jordan under Joshua, takes Jericho and much of Canaan, and divides the land among the twelve tribes; it ends with Joshua's charge to choose whom they will serve.
judges: The unsettled years after Joshua, told as a repeating cycle of falling away, oppression and rescue by leaders such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson, ending in disorder: every man did what was right in his own eyes.
ruth: A short story set in the time of the judges: the Moabite widow Ruth stays with her mother-in-law Naomi, gleans in the fields of Boaz in Bethlehem, and becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
1-samuel: The move from judges to kings: Samuel's birth and call, the rise and decline of Saul, Israel's first king, and the young David, from the fight with Goliath to years as an outlaw.
2-samuel: The reign of David: Jerusalem made the capital, the promise of a lasting dynasty, his sin with Bathsheba, and the troubles in his own family that follow, including Absalom's revolt.
1-kings: Solomon's wisdom and the building of the temple, the kingdom split in two after his death, and the kings of Israel and Judah, with the prophet Elijah standing against Ahab and Jezebel.
2-kings: The divided kingdoms to their ends: Elisha's ministry, the fall of Israel to Assyria, the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah in Judah, and the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon.
1-chronicles: History retold from Adam to David, opening with long genealogies and centred on David's reign and his preparations for the temple, written for those who returned from exile.
2-chronicles: The story of Solomon and the kings of Judah, told with an eye on the temple and its worship, ending with the exile and Cyrus's decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild.
ezra: The return from Babylon: the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem against opposition, and the scribe Ezra's arrival decades later to teach the law of Moses.
nehemiah: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, comes to Jerusalem to rebuild its broken walls, which are finished in fifty-two days; the people renew their covenant as Ezra reads the law.
esther: Set at the Persian court: the Jewish queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai foil Haman's plot to destroy their people, the origin of the feast of Purim. God is never named in it.
job: A poem framed by a story: Job, a righteous man, loses everything; his friends insist he must have sinned, Job demands an answer, and God at last speaks out of the whirlwind.
psalms: One hundred and fifty songs and prayers, many attributed to David: praise and lament, thanksgiving, confession and trust, long the prayer book of synagogue and church.
proverbs: Sayings on wisdom and folly, much of it attributed to Solomon: short observations on work, speech, money, friendship and family, ending with the portrait of the virtuous woman.
ecclesiastes: The reflections of the Preacher, who tried wisdom, pleasure and work and found all of it vanity under the sun; it holds the passage on a time for every purpose.
song-of-solomon: Love poetry: a dialogue between a woman and her beloved, full of gardens, vineyards and spices, read by some as human love and by many as an allegory of God's love.
isaiah: The prophet of Jerusalem in the eighth century BC: warnings to Judah and the nations, promises of a coming king and a suffering servant, and comfort for exiles, in some of the Bible's finest poetry.
jeremiah: The prophet of Judah's last decades, who warned of Babylon's coming, was imprisoned for it and saw Jerusalem fall; it also promises a new covenant written on the heart.
lamentations: Five poems of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, most of them acrostics, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah.
ezekiel: A priest among the exiles in Babylon, whose visions include the glory of God on wheeled creatures, the valley of dry bones, and a restored temple with a river flowing from it.
daniel: Stories of Daniel and his friends in the Babylonian and Persian courts, the fiery furnace and the lions' den, followed by visions of empires and the end of days.
hosea: The prophet's marriage to an unfaithful wife becomes a picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to God, and of a love that will not let her go.
joel: A plague of locusts becomes a call to repentance and a vision of the day of the LORD, with the promise that God will pour out his spirit upon all flesh.
amos: A herdsman from Judah sent to the prosperous northern kingdom to condemn its injustice to the poor: let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
obadiah: The shortest book of the Old Testament, a single chapter: an oracle against Edom for standing by when Jerusalem fell.
jonah: The prophet who ran from his call to warn Nineveh, was swallowed by a great fish, preached, and then sulked when the city repented and God spared it.
micah: A prophet from the countryside of Judah who condemned the powerful, foretold a ruler from Bethlehem, and summed up what God requires: to do justly, love mercy and walk humbly.
nahum: A poem celebrating the coming fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, which had long oppressed Israel and Judah.
habakkuk: The prophet questions God about injustice and about Babylon's rise, waits for an answer, and ends in a psalm of trust: the just shall live by his faith.
zephaniah: Prophecies from the reign of Josiah about the coming day of the LORD's judgment, ending with a promise that God will rejoice over his people with singing.
haggai: Short messages from 520 BC urging the returned exiles to stop building their own houses and finish rebuilding the temple.
zechariah: Night visions and prophecies encouraging the rebuilding of the temple, and looking ahead to a humble king riding into Jerusalem on a donkey.
malachi: The last of the prophets in the Christian Old Testament: disputes with priests and people over careless worship, ending with the promise that Elijah will come before the day of the LORD.
matthew: The gospel written with Jewish readers in mind, tracing Jesus' descent from Abraham and gathering his teaching into five discourses, among them the Sermon on the Mount.
mark: The shortest and probably the earliest gospel: a fast-moving account of Jesus' ministry in Galilee, his journey to Jerusalem, his death and the empty tomb.
luke: An orderly account of Jesus' life addressed to Theophilus, with the fullest story of his birth and parables found nowhere else, such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son.
john: The gospel that begins In the beginning was the Word: seven signs, long discourses, the I am sayings, and an extended account of Jesus' last night with his disciples.
acts: Luke's sequel: the church from the ascension and Pentecost in Jerusalem, through Peter and Stephen, to Paul's journeys around the Mediterranean and his arrival in Rome.
romans: Paul's fullest letter, written to a church he had not yet visited, setting out how Jew and Gentile alike are made righteous by faith, and how they should live together.
1-corinthians: Paul answers a divided, troubled church in Corinth on factions, lawsuits, marriage, worship and the resurrection; it includes the chapter on charity.
2-corinthians: Paul's most personal letter, defending his work against rivals in Corinth and writing of strength made perfect in weakness and of the collection for Jerusalem.
galatians: A sharp letter to churches in Galatia warning against requiring Gentile believers to keep the law of Moses, with a defence of Paul's own calling and of freedom in Christ.
ephesians: A letter on the church as one body of Jews and Gentiles, ending with practical counsel for households and the call to put on the whole armour of God.
philippians: A warm letter written from prison to the church at Philippi, thanking them for their gift and urging joy and unity, with the hymn of Christ who humbled himself.
colossians: A letter to a church in the Lycus valley about the supremacy of Christ, warning against philosophies and rules, with counsel for daily life.
1-thessalonians: Probably Paul's earliest surviving letter, to a young church in Thessalonica: encouragement in persecution and teaching on the Lord's coming.
2-thessalonians: A short follow-up letter correcting the belief that the day of the Lord had already come, and telling the idle to work for their bread.
1-timothy: Counsel to Paul's younger colleague in Ephesus on false teaching, worship, and the qualities to look for in bishops and deacons.
2-timothy: Paul's last letter, written from prison to Timothy as he expected death: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.
titus: Instructions to Titus on Crete about appointing elders, sound teaching, and good conduct among believers.
philemon: A one-chapter personal letter asking Philemon to welcome back Onesimus, his runaway slave, as a brother in Christ.
hebrews: A sermon-like letter of unknown author arguing that Christ is greater than angels, Moses and the priests of the old covenant, with the roll call of faith in chapter eleven.
james: A practical letter in the style of wisdom literature: on trials, the tongue, rich and poor, and faith that shows itself in works.
1-peter: A letter to scattered Christians in Asia Minor facing suffering, encouraging hope and good conduct among unbelievers.
2-peter: A short letter warning against false teachers and answering those who scoffed that the Lord's promised coming had not happened.
1-john: A letter on walking in the light, telling true teaching from false, and love: God is love, and he that loveth not knoweth not God.
2-john: A brief note to the elect lady and her children, urging love and warning against deceivers.
3-john: A brief personal note to Gaius, praising his hospitality to travelling teachers and complaining of Diotrephes.
jude: A short, vivid warning against false teachers who had crept into the church, ending with a well-known doxology.
revelation: John's visions on Patmos: letters to seven churches, the seals, trumpets and bowls, the beast and the fall of Babylon, and a new heaven and a new earth.
